title: Do You Run Away From Conflict?
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article addresses leaders who avoid conflict out of a need to be liked, and the cost that avoidance carries. It describes how conflict-averse leaders send vague, non-committal messages instead of honest feedback, leaving team members without the direction they need to improve. The piece is blunt that this avoidance amounts to a form of dishonesty that erodes trust and marks a leader as unreliable in the eyes of the team. Its central prescription is separating the person from the performance: affirming someone's value while still delivering candid feedback about their actions, starting with low-stakes situations to build the habit.
points: Leaders who avoid conflict often send ambiguous signals that get misread as 'everything is fine.'
Withholding honest feedback to avoid conflict is described as a form of dishonesty that undermines trust.
Avoiding conflict effectively pushes leadership responsibility onto others by leaving a performance vacuum.
The recommended fix is separating the person from the performance: affirm the individual's value while still giving candid feedback on their work.
Practicing candor on low-stakes issues first is suggested as a way to build comfort with conflict over time.
quotes: Working through conflict takes time, energy and courage. Dodging conflict or avoiding it altogether is always the path of least resistance.
For leaders allergic to conflict, delivering a tough message becomes a herculean task.
Perhaps the worst drawback for leaders who eschew conflict is the dishonesty required to avoid ruffling feathers.
The stamp of gutless rarely leaves a leader and undermines just about everything they do in the eyes of the team.
Separating the person and the performance is critical for all leaders, but especially for those who avoid conflict.
When they support the qualities of a team member but insist on offering candid feedback about their actions, others like them even more.
